title: Karan Johar Just Walked Into Malayalam Cinema — and He Brought a Shape-Shifter With Him
excerpt: Dharma Productions enters Kerala for the first time ever with 'Odiyan: The Age of Illusion,' a folklore horror starring Prithviraj Sukumaran and Manju Warrier, directed by the man who made Bramayugam.
body:
There is a moment in every production house's life when it stops expanding and starts exploring. For **Karan Johar's Dharma Productions** — the studio that practically invented the modern Bollywood family drama, that gave us *Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham* and *Ae Dil Hai Mushkil* and a thousand sequined wedding sequences — that moment arrived on June 16, 2026, with a single Instagram post and a poster that looked nothing like anything Dharma has ever made.

No sequins. No snow. No Tuscany.

Just a round baroque frame, the skeletal remains of a small horned creature, and two words in a font that felt like it had crawled out of a Kerala forest at midnight: **Odiyan**.

## What Is an Odiyan?

In the folklore of northern Kerala, the Odiyan is a figure of terror — a practitioner of dark sorcery who can shapeshift, usually into an animal, to move unseen through the night. Part assassin, part phantom, the Odiyan legend has been whispered across Malabar households for generations, the kind of story grandmothers told to keep children indoors after dark. It is primal, it is specific to Kerala's cultural landscape, and it has never been given the full Bollywood production treatment.

Until now.

*Odiyan: The Age of Illusion* is set in 19th-century Kerala and tells the story of a shape-shifter whose fury descends on a powerful matriarchal household, setting off what the makers describe as "a battle between truth and illusion that crackles with myth, menace and psychological weight." Directed by **Rahul Sadasivan** — the filmmaker behind *Bhoothakaalam*, the Mammootty-starrer *Bramayugam*, and the Pranav Mohanlal horror *Diés Irae* — it stars **Prithviraj Sukumaran** and **Manju Warrier**, two of Malayalam cinema's most formidable presences.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DZosu_rCMDn/

If Sadasivan's name doesn't immediately register, it should. *Bramayugam* was one of 2024's most critically celebrated Indian films — a period horror set inside a haunted manor, performed almost entirely by Mammootty, and built on atmosphere rather than jump scares. It proved that Malayalam horror could be literary, slow-burning, and genuinely unsettling. *Odiyan* is Sadasivan's most ambitious project yet, and having Dharma's resources behind it means the scale will match the ambition.

## Why Dharma? Why Now?

> "I have been a great admirer of Malayalam cinema for a long time. The craft, the courage, the way its filmmakers trust their audiences — it is something I have watched with genuine awe." — Karan Johar

Johar's statement reads less like corporate diplomacy and more like a genuine creative confession. Malayalam cinema has spent the last five years building a reputation as India's most consistently daring film industry — from *Minnal Murali* to *Manjummel Boys* to *Bramayugam* — while Bollywood has often struggled to match that inventiveness. For Dharma to choose a folklore horror as its entry point, rather than a glossy romance or a star vehicle, signals that this isn't a vanity expansion. It's a creative bet.

The production credentials reinforce this. Co-producing alongside Johar are **Adar Poonawalla** (yes, the Serum Institute heir, increasingly active in entertainment), **Apoorva Mehta** (Dharma's CEO), and **Supriya Menon** from Prithviraj Productions. This is a genuine partnership, not a Bollywood takeover.

## The Cast Is Perfect

**Prithviraj Sukumaran** has been on a remarkable run — *Aadujeevitham*, *L2: Empuraan*, and his work as both actor and producer have cemented him as Malayalam cinema's most versatile leading man. He brings both commercial appeal and the dramatic weight a story like this demands.

**Manju Warrier** needs no introduction to anyone who has watched Indian cinema with open eyes. Her return to acting after a long hiatus in 2014's *How Old Are You?* was one of the decade's great comebacks, and every role since has confirmed what everyone already knew: she is one of the finest actresses the country has ever produced.

Pairing them in a folklore horror directed by the man who turned a single room and Mammootty's face into 90 minutes of dread? That is the kind of casting announcement that makes you sit up.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

Malayalam cinema already has a devoted NRI audience — the Gulf, North America, the UK. But Dharma's involvement changes the distribution game entirely. Expect *Odiyan* to receive the kind of international release typically reserved for Hindi tentpoles — wide multiplex rollouts, IMAX screenings, and the marketing muscle that comes with one of India's biggest production houses.

For Malayali diaspora audiences, this is their folklore, their legend, rendered with the production values it deserves. For everyone else, it is a window into one of India's richest and most underexplored mythological traditions — the kind of story that Hollywood would turn into a prestige horror series, but that only Kerala can tell with authenticity.

No release date yet. But the poster is already on Johar's wall, and the forests of 19th-century Malabar are waiting.

Something ancient just got a very modern megaphone.
